docs.title: Writing a lab (internal template)
docs.text:
This page is for whoever writes and proofs the labs. Students do not need it.

Every lab follows the same seven sections. Change the shape only when a module genuinely cannot fit it, and record the reason in the verification file.

docs.title: A · Requirement
docs.text: One short paragraph giving the requirement: the protection the app is supposed to provide, in plain terms, with no sign of whether it holds. A second short paragraph says what to run against the installed app. Leave out the location, tool names that give the approach away, and any explanation of the vulnerability.

docs.title: B · Validation
docs.text:
Numbered, literal, and runnable exactly as written.

  • Use the exact UI labels from app-vulnerable, including case, punctuation, and numbering.
  • Put exact commands in fenced bash blocks. One command per block when order matters.
  • Every command that can fail gets an Expected line showing the shape of the output.
  • When a command needs something from an earlier step, say so ("the path from step 6").
  • If a step needs root, Wi-Fi, or a second terminal, say it in that step.
  • The shell is Git Bash on Windows. Add a macOS/Linux note only where commands differ.
  • The employee must not read the source code. Even when the source is the easiest way to see the issue, route the finding through the running app or the installed package.
  • The finding is the employee's own work. Route it through their own commands against the installed package or the running app. The app's built-in vector buttons and the module's poc/ scripts may appear only after the manual finding, as confirmation or automation. A script step is marked optional when it needs the project repository.
  • When the vulnerability lives in the app file itself (hardcoded secrets, embedded files), prefer package analysis. The learner pulls the file apart and the app's screens stay closed.

docs.title: C · Questions
docs.text: Three questions maximum, all requiring the employee to write something. No yes/no questions. The questions should make them state what they observed, where exactly it was, and why it matters.

docs.title: D · Finding
docs.text: An objective checkpoint: the same fact confirmed through two independent channels (runtime against static, app against file, vulnerable against secure). When the finding lives entirely in the app package (hardcoded secrets, embedded files), the two channels are the employee's manual extraction and an independent check of the same artifact, for example the module's script. Give the employee a table or checklist that says when the finding is complete. Leave interpretation out of it.

docs.title: E · Evidence
docs.text: Exactly what gets handed in: screenshot prompts that name the artifact, plus a description template of two or three sentences. Keep it short. The evidence is the deliverable, not a report.

docs.title: F · Hints
docs.text: At most three ordered hints. Hints fix the environment or the procedure and never reveal the value or the conclusion. Prefer commands the employee can run to diagnose (adb devices, ls, re-run the step) over explanations.

docs.title: G · Explanation
docs.text:
Behind a collapsible block, guarded by "open only after your evidence":

  • the CWE and MASWE mapping,
  • why the finding matters, with concrete impact,
  • what the :app-secure counterpart does,
  • links to the reference page, POC scripts, and the relevant MASTG test. Name the script paths and the exact command to run them.

docs.title: File and nav conventions
docs.text:
What Where Lab file docs/labs/lab-NN-<slug>.md, where NN is the MASWE number Setup lab docs/labs/setup.md (Lab 00, shared by all labs) Index row docs/labs/index.md, table at the bottom Nav entry mkdocs.yml, under 🧪 Hands-on Labs Proof checklist docs/labs/verification/lab-NN.md, not added to the nav

Each lab starts with the metadata table (module, category, CWE, time, level, needs) and links back to the reference page under docs/maswe/.

Status values in the index:

  • 🧪 Awaiting proof run: written, not yet run end to end on a clean emulator.
  • ✅ Ready: every step confirmed in one clean run.
  • ⚠️ Known issue: a step is known to fail in some environments; the note says which.

docs.title: POC scripts in labs
docs.text:
Each feature module may ship scripts under features/<module>/poc/. In a lab they are allowed only as a confirmation stage after the manual finding, never as the way the finding is made.

Before a script appears in a lab, test it against the real app:

  • The package id must be com.hasantuncay.mobsec. The original adb_verify.sh targeted com.hasantuncay.mobsec.vulnerable, a package that exists on no device.
  • The patterns must match the module's planted values. The same script missed every mock_secret_ style value until it was fixed.
  • It must run on Git Bash. Check unzip, mktemp, and grep -a before the step ships.

If a script cannot find the module's motif, fix the script or leave it out. A confirmation step that reports nothing is worse than no step.

docs.title: Proof protocol (run before a lab is marked ✅)
docs.text:
1. Start clean. Cold-boot the emulator, run adb uninstall com.hasantuncay.mobsec, then reinstall the APK. Do not reuse a session from earlier work.
  2. Run Lab 00 first, exactly as written. If setup fails, the lab cannot be proven.
  3. Run the lab literally. Follow the steps in order without using your knowledge of the code. Type the commands from the page, not from memory.
  4. Record each step. In the verification file, mark pass or fail and note any difference in labels, paths, output text, or timing.
  5. Run every optional step once too, in the same session, including the module's POC script pointed at both the pulled APK and the installed app. A script that reports nothing is broken; fix it or the step before shipping.
  6. Fix the lab, not the note. If a step behaves differently, rewrite the step. A difference that cannot be avoided goes into a !!! note block on the lab page.
  7. Record the environment: emulator product and image (Android Studio AVD or Genymotion), API level, host OS, terminal (Git Bash, zsh, PowerShell), and whether the app came from a provided APK or a local build.
  8. Only after a full clean pass: change the index status to ✅ and date the verification file.

If a lab cannot be finished because the app itself is incomplete (missing screen, dead button), record it as a ⚠️ known issue and open a repo issue. The lab does not ship as ✅.

docs.title: Lab 01: The Token That Stayed in Plain Sight
docs.text:
Module MASWE-0001: Sensitive Data Stored Unencrypted in Private Storage Category MASVS-STORAGE CWE CWE-312: Cleartext Storage of Sensitive Information Time ~25 minutes Level Beginner Needs Lab rules read · Lab 00: Setup complete · 🎯 MobSec Victim installed · adb working

Self-paced lab

Tap the demo buttons to create the test data, then inspect the files from your terminal. Use your command output as evidence. Section E lists what to submit.

docs.title: A · Requirement
docs.text:
The app stores a signed access token that authenticates the user. It should keep the token where nothing outside the app can read it, and its encryption keys should be just as private.

Store a token in the app and check whether you can read it from disk. For the encrypted record, locate the key and check whether the same access lets you read it too.

The demo buttons may display file paths and a result summary. Verify those claims by inspecting the files yourself.

Do not read the project source code. Use the installed app and your terminal.

docs.title: B · Validation
docs.text: Run everything in one terminal (Git Bash on Windows). This lab needs the emulator running and the app installed.

docs.title: 1. Take a "before" reading
docs.text:
List the app's own file storage before you touch the app:

adb shell run-as com.hasantuncay.mobsec ls -la files
adb shell run-as com.hasantuncay.mobsec ls -la files/datastore

run-as opens the app's private folder as the app itself. It works because Lab 00 installs a debug build. On a normal phone, the same read needs root.

Expected: the first command lists a short set of entries, or prints No such file or directory. The second usually prints No such file or directory. Save this output so you can compare it with the listing after the write.

The app writes a result card after every button

Leave the result card unread until you have inspected the files. Capture your terminal output for the evidence in section E.

docs.title: 2. Make the app store the value
docs.text:
Open 🎯 MobSec Victim. The dashboard groups modules by category. Tap MASVS-STORAGE to expand it:

Then open the MASWE-0001 row.

Incorrect dashboard subtitle

The row subtitle reads MASWE-0001: Private Storage (SECURE). That wording is a bug in this training build. The screen title bar is what counts, and it says MASWE-0001 (VULNERABLE).

The module screen lists six vectors. This lab uses the first and the third:

Tap the first button: 1. Data Stored Unencrypted (Cleartext).

docs.title: 3. Look again
docs.text:
adb shell run-as com.hasantuncay.mobsec ls -la files
adb shell run-as com.hasantuncay.mobsec ls -la files/datastore

Expected: files now contains a datastore directory, and inside it is one file, maswe0001_v1.preferences_pb. Some DataStore versions also leave a small lock file next to it; this one does not. Owner, size, and date are whatever your emulator reports; the name is the part that matters.

-rw------- 1 u0_a2XX u0_a2XX  1234 2026-..-.. ..:.. maswe0001_v1.preferences_pb

Compare this with step 1 to identify the file created by the button tap.

docs.title: 4. Read the stored value
docs.text:
The file is not plain text; it is a protobuf blob with the token embedded. grep with -a reads it as text and keeps the readable run:

adb exec-out run-as com.hasantuncay.mobsec cat files/datastore/maswe0001_v1.preferences_pb | grep -a eyJ

Expected: a single line containing auth_token and a value that begins with eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9. A few unprintable bytes from the protobuf wrapper may sit around it. Copy the eyJ... run into your notes exactly; in this training data it ends with three dots.

If grep prints nothing, check the file path and tap the vector again. Wait two seconds, then rerun the command.

docs.title: 5. Create an encrypted record
docs.text: Go back to the app screen and tap the third button: 3. Encryption Key Stored on Filesystem.

docs.title: 6. Locate the encrypted record and key file
docs.text:
adb shell run-as com.hasantuncay.mobsec ls -la files
adb shell run-as com.hasantuncay.mobsec ls -la shared_prefs

Expected: files gained maswe0001_v3.enc, and shared_prefs gained maswe0001_v3_keys.xml. These contain the encrypted record and its key, respectively. Ignore unrelated XML files from earlier app starts.

docs.title: 7. Read the key
docs.text:
adb shell "run-as com.hasantuncay.mobsec cat shared_prefs/maswe0001_v3_keys.xml"

Expected: a small XML file with one entry, <string name="aes_key"> followed by a long base64 value. That value is the AES key the app used for maswe0001_v3.enc. It sits in the same storage, one folder over, in the clear.

docs.title: 8. Optional: let the project's checker confirm it
docs.text:
If you have the project repository on this machine, the module ships a script that looks for the same two artifacts:

bash features/maswe0001/poc/adb_verify.sh

Expected: [!] CRITICAL VULNERABILITY CONFIRMED (MASWE-0001 / CWE-312): followed by the files it could read, including the one from step 4. The script also checks files from other storage vectors. Those additional results are not required for this lab.

docs.title: C · Questions
docs.text:
Answer these in your notes before moving on:

  1. ✍️ The datastore folder lives inside the app's private storage. Who can normally read that folder on a real phone, and what made it readable for you without root?
  2. ✍️ Vector 3 did encrypt the data. Explain in your own words why the finding stands anyway: where did the key end up, and what does that mean for someone holding a copy of the device storage?
  3. ✍️ What can an attacker do with the value you pulled out in step 4? Name one concrete action.

docs.title: D · Finding
docs.text:
You have the finding when all four are true:

Test What it shows The step 3 listing A new file appeared in the app's private storage right after the app processed data The step 4 output The app stored a usable token in cleartext, readable byte for byte, with no decryption step anywhere The steps 6 and 7 outputs The app's encrypted file keeps its AES key in a separate file in the same private storage Section C, question 3 One sentence of impact: what an attacker does with what they read

If you ran step 8, its output is a second, independent confirmation of the same files. Attach it as well.

docs.title: E · Evidence
docs.text:
Hand in:

  1. 📷 Screenshot 1: your terminal with the step 3 listing and the step 4 output. The token value must be readable, not cut off.
  2. 📷 Screenshot 2: the step 6 listing and the step 7 key file.
  3. ✍️ Two or three sentences, in your own words:
  4. what was stored without encryption and where,
  5. why storing the key this way leaves the encrypted record exposed,
  6. one concrete thing an attacker could do with the token.

Submit these through your training channel. No long report is needed.

docs.title: F · Hints
docs.text:
Hint 1: the app or the buttons are not where I expect
  • The dashboard groups modules under category cards. Expand MASVS-STORAGE first.
  • The row subtitle may mention SECURE; ignore it and check the screen title bar for MASWE-0001 (VULNERABLE).
  • Only buttons 1 and 3 matter for this lab. If a tap produces no visible change, tap it again and give the app a second to write.
Hint 2: storage looks empty or different from the page
  • List first, tap second, list again third: step 1 records the snapshot, step 3 shows the change.
  • run-as: package not debuggable means the release build is installed. Reinstall the debug APK from Lab 00.
  • ls may print No such file or directory for files/datastore until vector 1 has run once.
Hint 3: the cat output is noisy or empty
  • The DataStore file is binary with the token inside. Run the step 4 pipe exactly as written: adb exec-out ... | grep -a eyJ.
  • If the pipe prints a warning about binary data, you dropped the -a. It is the flag that keeps the matches readable.
  • The XML key file is plain text, so step 7 needs no pipe. If it prints nothing, the vector 3 tap did not land.

docs.title: G · Explanation
docs.text:
Open only after sections C and E are done

Complete your answers and capture your evidence before opening the explanation.

What happened on disk

MASWE-0001 covers CWE-312: Cleartext Storage of Sensitive Information.

Vector 1 wrote an OAuth-style bearer token into a Jetpack DataStore file (files/datastore/maswe0001_v1.preferences_pb) without encryption. The protobuf format stores readable token bytes, which is why the text search recovered the value.

Vector 3 encrypted the record with AES but stored the AES key in shared_prefs/maswe0001_v3_keys.xml. Access to both locations allows an attacker to copy the ciphertext and the key needed to decrypt it. Root malware or a forensic image can provide that access, as did your inspection of this debug build.

The module demonstrates four more storage habits on its other buttons: a key hardcoded in the app package, AES in ECB mode, a FileProvider whose path config maps far more of the filesystem than it should, and a cache file that is never deleted.

Why it matters:

  • Tokens recovered from storage authenticate as the user until they expire or are revoked.
  • Private storage restricts ordinary app access. Root access, a device image, or debugging access can still expose the files, so sensitive data needs encryption with a separately protected key.
  • Copying both the key file and the encrypted record defeats the protection demonstrated in vector 3.

What the secure app does instead:

The :app-secure implementation keeps its encryption keys in the Android Keystore and wraps storage with Tink AEAD (AndroidKeystore master key, encrypted DataStore serializer). Vector 3's secure counterpart uses envelope encryption, with the key-encrypting key in hardware and only a wrapped data key on disk.

Go deeper:

  • Reference page: MASWE-0001: Sensitive Data Stored Unencrypted in Private Storage
  • The vulnerable code lives in features/maswe0001/src/main/java/com/hasantuncay/mobsec/maswe0001/vulnerable/Maswe0001VulnerableRepository.kt.
  • The module's automation is in features/maswe0001/poc/: a Semgrep rule for CI scanning, a Frida hook for runtime inspection, and the adb script from step 8.

docs.title: Lab 02: Outside the Sandbox
docs.text:
Module MASWE-0002: Sensitive Data Stored Unencrypted Outside of Private Storage Category MASVS-STORAGE CWE CWE-732: Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource Time ~25 minutes Level Beginner Needs Lab rules read · Lab 00: Setup complete · 🎯 MobSec Victim installed · adb working

Self-paced lab

Inspect the files created by the demo buttons, then copy a record to your machine. The commands use the adb shell user; see Hint 1 if your emulator restricts access to the folder. Section E lists what to submit.

docs.title: A · Requirement
docs.text:
The app keeps sensitive records on the device, and it should keep them inside its own sandbox, where other apps cannot reach. Shared storage, the part of the device a PC can reach over USB, is not a place for anything sensitive.

Create a record and inspect its location, contents, and permissions. Copy it off the device, then check whether the encrypted record's key is accessible in the same location.

Do not read the project source code. Use the installed app and your terminal.

docs.title: B · Validation
docs.text:
Run everything in one terminal (Git Bash on Windows) and one folder of your choice.

Do not tap the DOCS button

The DOCS button opens the official OWASP explanation. Read it after completing your checks and capturing the evidence.

docs.title: 1. Look before
docs.text:
adb shell ls -la /sdcard/Android/data/com.hasantuncay.mobsec/files/

Expected on a fresh install: No such file or directory. The folder is created together with the app's first write. /sdcard is an alias for /storage/emulated/0; both spellings work.

docs.title: 2. Make the app write outside its sandbox
docs.text:
Open 🎯 MobSec Victim, expand MASVS-STORAGE, and open the MASWE-0002 row.

Incorrect dashboard subtitle

The row subtitle may read MASWE-0002: Insecure Storage (SECURE). That is a bug in this training build. The screen title bar is what counts: MASWE-0002 (VULNERABLE).

The module lists five vectors. This lab needs the first and the third:

Tap the first button: 1. External Storage Sensitive Data Leak. Ignore the app's result card, and leave DOCS alone.

docs.title: 3. Look again
docs.text:
adb shell ls -la /sdcard/Android/data/com.hasantuncay.mobsec/files/

Expected: the folder now exists and lists one file, maswe0002_plaintext.json. Owner and size are whatever your emulator reports.

docs.title: 4. Read the record
docs.text:
adb shell cat /sdcard/Android/data/com.hasantuncay.mobsec/files/maswe0002_plaintext.json

Expected: a small JSON object with two fields. auth_token holds a value that starts with eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9 and ends with three dots, and pan holds a 16-digit card number that starts with 4532.

Record which access you used

If the command succeeded without the Hint 1 fallback, the adb shell user could read the file without root or run-as.

The result card's claim about API 29 refers to access by ordinary apps. Shell access can differ; record whether your emulator required the Hint 1 fallback.

docs.title: 5. Take it off the device
docs.text:
adb pull /sdcard/Android/data/com.hasantuncay.mobsec/files/maswe0002_plaintext.json .
cat maswe0002_plaintext.json

Expected: 1 file pulled, 0 skipped. followed by the same JSON, now sitting on your machine. Newer adb versions print the source path and a transfer rate around that line.

docs.title: 6. Create the encrypted record
docs.text:
Go back to the module screen and tap the third button: 3. External Storage + Key on Filesystem. Then:

adb shell ls -la /sdcard/Android/data/com.hasantuncay.mobsec/files/

Expected: two new files, maswe0002_key_on_fs.enc and maswe0002_secret.key.

docs.title: 7. Read the key
docs.text:
adb shell od -An -tx1 /sdcard/Android/data/com.hasantuncay.mobsec/files/maswe0002_secret.key

Expected: two lines of hex bytes, 32 in total. That is the AES key for the .enc file sitting next to it, written to the same shared folder. Run the same command on maswe0002_key_on_fs.enc if you want to see the ciphertext it protects.

docs.title: 8. Optional: let the project's checker confirm it
docs.text:
If you have the project repository on this machine, the module ships a script that repeats the key parts of this inspection:

bash features/maswe0002/poc/adb_verify.sh

Expected: [!] CRITICAL VULNERABILITY CONFIRMED (MASWE-0002 / CWE-732): followed by the plaintext record it could read from /sdcard/Android/data/... and the key file it found beside the ciphertext.

docs.title: C · Questions
docs.text:
Answer these in your notes before moving on:

  1. ✍️ Lab 01 used run-as to read private files. Which access did you use here, including any Hint 1 fallback? Compare the two storage locations and who can reach them on a real device.
  2. ✍️ Where did vector 3 store its encryption key? Explain what access to that file means for the encrypted record.
  3. ✍️ You copied the record off the device in one command. Name one concrete thing an attacker can do with it.

docs.title: D · Finding
docs.text:
You have the finding when all four are true:

Test What it shows The step 1 and step 3 listings A file appeared outside the app's private sandbox, minutes after the app wrote it The step 4 output A readable token and card number; record whether the shell read succeeded directly or needed the Hint 1 fallback The step 5 output A copy of the record now exists on your machine, pulled with one command The steps 6 and 7 outputs The encrypted file and its readable AES key are in the same shared folder

If you ran step 8, its output is a second, independent confirmation of the same artifacts. Attach it as well.

docs.title: E · Evidence
docs.text:
Hand in:

  1. 📷 Screenshot 1: your terminal with the step 3 listing and the step 4 output. The token and the card number must be readable, not cut off.
  2. 📷 Screenshot 2: the step 6 listing and the step 7 hex key, or the step 5 pull and host-side cat.
  3. ✍️ Two or three sentences, in your own words:
  4. what was written and to which kind of storage,
  5. why the encrypted file does not fix the problem,
  6. one concrete thing an attacker could do with the record.

Submit these through your training channel. No long report is needed.

docs.title: F · Hints
docs.text:
Hint 1: Permission denied on the folder
  • Some emulator images restrict /sdcard/Android/data from the shell user. If yours does and it allows adb root (images without the Play Store do; Lab 00's default), run it, wait for the restart, then repeat the command.
  • This only applies to the read steps. If step 1 printed No such file or directory, that is not a permission problem; the folder simply does not exist yet.
Hint 2: the folder is still missing after the tap
  • Confirm the tap landed: the button turns red and the app shows a result card you were told to ignore.
  • Wait a second and list again. The directory is created with the first write.
  • Check the package name in the path: com.hasantuncay.mobsec, no .vulnerable suffix.
Hint 3: od or cat misbehaves
  • od is a standard part of the device shell. If it fails anyway, pull the file and inspect it on your machine: adb pull .../maswe0002_secret.key . then od -An -tx1 maswe0002_secret.key.
  • The JSON file is plain text, so cat is enough for it. If the output looks garbled, you are reading the wrong file.

docs.title: G · Explanation
docs.text:
Open only after sections C and E are done

Complete your answers and capture your evidence before opening the explanation.

Why the folder was readable

MASWE-0002 applies CWE-732: Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource to sensitive files outside private storage.

Every vector in this module writes through getExternalFilesDir(), which lands in /sdcard/Android/data/com.hasantuncay.mobsec/files/. This is an app-specific directory on shared storage, outside the private sandbox. The JSON holds an unencrypted auth token and card number. On the emulator used to verify this lab, the adb shell user could read it directly; some images require the root fallback in Hint 1. Older Android versions also allowed access by other apps holding storage permission.

Vector 3 encrypted the payload with AES and wrote its 32-byte key to maswe0002_secret.key in the same folder. A reader with access to both files can decrypt the payload. The other buttons demonstrate a hardcoded key, DES with the literal key WeakKey1, and a key derived from ANDROID_ID, which is stable per device and not a secret.

Why it matters:

  • Card numbers and tokens are regulated data. PCI-DSS treats readable storage as a finding on its own.
  • A record in shared storage leaves the device easily: a file manager, a USB connection, a backup tool, or one adb pull.
  • Once copied, deleting the app or the file does not retract any copy.
  • The encrypted record remains exposed to anyone who can copy its key from the shared folder.

What the secure app does instead:

The :app-secure implementation writes through Jetpack Security's EncryptedFile (AES-256-GCM with an HKDF-derived key), with the master key held in the Android Keystore, and keeps the one plaintext copy inside the private sandbox. The key never leaves hardware-backed storage.

Go deeper:

  • Reference page: MASWE-0002: Sensitive Data Stored Unencrypted Outside of Private Storage
  • The vulnerable code lives in features/maswe0002/src/main/java/com/hasantuncay/mobsec/maswe0002/vulnerable/Maswe0002VulnerableRepository.kt.
  • The module's automation is in features/maswe0002/poc/: a Semgrep rule pack for CI, a Frida hook for runtime inspection, and the adb script from step 8.

docs.title: Lab 03: The Spare Key Under the Mat
docs.text:
Module MASWE-0003: Cryptographic Keys Stored Outside of Platform Keystore Category MASVS-STORAGE · MASVS-CRYPTO CWE CWE-312: Cleartext Storage of Sensitive Information Time ~25 minutes Level Beginner Needs Lab rules read · Lab 00: Setup complete · 🎯 MobSec Victim installed · adb working

Self-paced lab

Use the demo buttons to generate and import key material, then inspect the resulting files and logs. Section E lists the evidence to submit.

docs.title: A · Requirement
docs.text:
The app should use the Android Keystore to protect its cryptographic keys. The app can request operations with a Keystore key without reading or exporting the key bytes. Raw keys should not appear in preferences files or logs.

Inspect the two locations used by this app and check whether they contain key bytes or a reference to a protected key. Explain what an attacker could do with the material you recover.

Do not read the project source code. Use the installed app and your terminal.

docs.title: B · Validation
docs.text: Run everything in one terminal (Git Bash on Windows). Capture the command output rather than the app's result cards.

docs.title: 1. Look before
docs.text:
adb shell run-as com.hasantuncay.mobsec ls -la shared_prefs

Expected: a short listing, or No such file or directory if this is your first storage lab. Save the output to compare with step 3.

docs.title: 2. Make the app store its key
docs.text:
Open 🎯 MobSec Victim, expand MASVS-STORAGE, and open the MASWE-0003 row.

Incorrect dashboard subtitle

The row subtitle may read something with SECURE in it. That is a bug in this training build. The screen title bar is what counts: MASWE-0003 (VULNERABLE).

The module lists three vectors. This lab needs the first and the third:

Inspect the output before reading the result cards

After each tap the card prints the path or the log command you are meant to find. Treat it as a spoiler: run your own commands first, and read the card only if you are stuck.

Tap the first button: 1. Key in SharedPreferences / File.

docs.title: 3. Look again
docs.text:
adb shell run-as com.hasantuncay.mobsec ls -la shared_prefs

Expected: a new SharedPreferences file named crypto_key.xml.

docs.title: 4. Read the stored key
docs.text:
adb shell "run-as com.hasantuncay.mobsec cat shared_prefs/crypto_key.xml"

Expected: a small XML file with one entry, <string name="aes_key"> followed by a base64 value. The value sits on one line, and a trailing encoded newline (
) and spaces can follow inside the element; the next command handles that. The app generated an AES key and wrote the encoded bytes straight to disk. The write is asynchronous, so if the entry is missing, wait a second and read again.

docs.title: 5. Decode and count the key bytes
docs.text:
Decode the stored value and check its length:

adb exec-out run-as com.hasantuncay.mobsec cat shared_prefs/crypto_key.xml | grep -o -E '[A-Za-z0-9+/]{40,}={0,2}' | head -n 1 | base64 -d | wc -c

The grep pulls the base64 run out of the XML, the decoder turns it back into bytes, and wc -c counts them.

Expected: 32, the byte length of an AES-256 key. The app stored the encoded key bytes, so a reader can decode and use them.

docs.title: 6. Inspect the imported key in the log
docs.text:
Clear earlier log entries before running the import:

adb logcat -c

Now go back to the module screen and tap the third button: 3. Plaintext Key Import.

Then dump the log:

adb logcat -d -s MASWE_0003_KEY_IMPORT

Expected: a line reading Importing key: followed by a plain, readable string. That is key material written into the system log for anyone with log access to find. If the dump is empty, tap the button again and rerun the command immediately.

docs.title: 7. Optional: let the project's checker confirm it
docs.text:
If you have the project repository on this machine, the module ships a script that repeats both reads:

bash features/maswe0003/poc/adb_verify.sh

Expected: [!] CRITICAL VULNERABILITY CONFIRMED (MASWE-0003 / CWE-312): followed by the key file it could read (with its decoded byte length) and the log line it found.

docs.title: C · Questions
docs.text:
Answer these in your notes before moving on:

  1. ✍️ The AES key existed as 32 readable bytes in a file. Where do app keys normally live on Android, and what is different about them there?
  2. ✍️ The log line is one adb command away while a device is attached for debugging. Name one more way log lines leave a device in normal operation.
  3. ✍️ With the key from step 4 in hand, what can an attacker do that they could not do without it? Name one concrete action.

docs.title: D · Finding
docs.text:
You have the finding when all four are true:

Test What it shows The step 3 listing A preferences file appeared minutes after the app generated a key The step 4 output The file holds a full base64 copy of the AES key, in the clear The step 5 output The copy decodes to 32 bytes of raw key material, ready to use The step 6 output More key material landed in the system log, readable with one command

If you ran step 7, its output is a second, independent confirmation of the same artifacts. Attach it as well.

docs.title: E · Evidence
docs.text:
Hand in:

  1. 📷 Screenshot 1: your terminal with the step 4 XML output and the step 5 32 result on screen.
  2. 📷 Screenshot 2: the step 6 log line.
  3. ✍️ Two or three sentences, in your own words:
  4. where the two copies of key material ended up,
  5. what the Keystore would have done differently,
  6. one concrete thing an attacker could do with a copied key.

Submit these through your training channel. No long report is needed.

docs.title: F · Hints
docs.text:
Hint 1: run-as or the file read fails
  • run-as: package not debuggable means the release build is installed. Reinstall the debug APK from Lab 00.
  • No such file or directory for shared_prefs means the button has not run yet. Tap 1. Key in SharedPreferences / File and list again.
Hint 2: the XML is there but the entry looks odd
  • The write is asynchronous. Wait one second, then cat again.
  • The value is base64, so it can contain +, /, and =. Copy it whole if you want to decode it by hand.
  • If you are on macOS instead of Git Bash, base64 -d may need to be base64 -D.
Hint 3: the logcat dump is empty
  • Clear the buffer first (adb logcat -c), tap the third button, then dump immediately. Busy emulators rotate the buffer quickly.
  • The tag is exact: MASWE_0003_KEY_IMPORT, with underscores.
  • Still empty, try without the filter: adb logcat -d | grep MASWE_0003.

docs.title: G · Explanation
docs.text:
Open only after sections C and E are done

Complete your answers and capture your evidence before opening the explanation.

Why the key left copies behind

This is MASWE-0003, covering CWE-312 (cleartext storage) and CWE-321 (hardcoded cryptographic key).

Vector 1 generated a fresh AES-256 key, encoded it with Base64.DEFAULT, and stored it in shared_prefs/crypto_key.xml under the name aes_key. Base64 encoding leaves the key recoverable by anyone who can read the file. Vector 3 passed key material to Log.d, exposing it to debugging sessions, bug reports, and logging pipelines.

Vector 2 hardcodes a key as a byte array in the app's bytecode. This copy ships in the app package and can be recovered with tools such as jadx or apktool.

Why it matters:

  • A device image can expose the preferences key, collected logs can expose the imported key, and the APK contains the hardcoded key from vector 2.
  • Keys outside the Keystore lose the hardware protections: attestation, non-exportability, and the option to require user authentication.
  • Rotating the app's key does not remove copies already collected from files, logs, or packages.

What the secure app does instead:

The :app-secure implementation generates its keys inside the Android Keystore (KeyGenerator.getInstance(KEY_ALGORITHM_AES, "AndroidKeyStore")), with StrongBox preferred where the hardware offers it, and nothing is written to preferences or logs. For keys that must arrive from a server, it points at Keystore wrapped key import instead of shipping raw material.

Go deeper:

  • Reference page: MASWE-0003: Cryptographic Keys Stored Outside of Platform Keystore
  • The vulnerable code lives in features/maswe0003/src/main/java/com/hasantuncay/mobsec/maswe0003/vulnerable/Maswe0003VulnerableRepository.kt.
  • The module's automation is in features/maswe0003/poc/: a Semgrep rule pack for CI, a Frida hook for runtime inspection, and the adb script from step 7.

docs.title: Lab 04: The Key That Never Left the Office
docs.text:
Module MASWE-0004: Sensitive Data Hardcoded in the App Package Category MASVS-STORAGE · MASVS-CRYPTO CWE CWE-798: Use of Hard-coded Credentials Time ~25 minutes Level Beginner Needs Lab rules read · Lab 00: Setup complete · 🎯 MobSec Victim installed · adb working

Self-paced lab

Inspect the installed APK for a payment secret. You can complete this lab without opening the app or reading its source code. Section E lists what to submit.

docs.title: A · Requirement
docs.text:
The app should not contain a reusable backend secret in its package. Anyone who obtains the APK can inspect its contents. Access credentials should be obtained at runtime, with a limited lifetime.

Pull the app off your emulator and look through the package with your own commands. Recover the payment secret, then explain in your own words what an attacker could do with it.

You do not need to open the app on the emulator for these checks.

Do not read the project source code. Work from the installed package.

docs.title: B · Validation
docs.text: Run everything in one terminal (Git Bash on Windows) and one folder that you choose.

docs.title: 1. Find the app file on the device
docs.text:
adb shell pm path com.hasantuncay.mobsec

Expected: one or more lines that start with package: and end in .apk. If the app was installed as a split APK, use the line that ends in base.apk. Copy everything after package:.

docs.title: 2. Copy the app file to your machine
docs.text:
adb pull <the path from step 1> case0004.apk

Expected: 1 file pulled.

No root needed

The installed app file is readable by the shell user, so this lab works on any emulator, rooted or not.

docs.title: 3. Unpack the app file
docs.text:
An APK is a ZIP archive. Unpack it:

unzip -o case0004.apk -d case0004
ls case0004

Expected: a listing with AndroidManifest.xml, resources.arsc, and one or more classes.dex files. The app's code compiles into the classes*.dex files.

Windows without unzip

If Git Bash says unzip: command not found, rename case0004.apk to case0004.zip, extract it with Windows Explorer into a folder named case0004, and continue with step 4.

docs.title: 4. Turn the compiled code into readable text
docs.text:
The dex file is binary, but the strings inside it are plain text. Extract the readable runs:

grep -a -h -o -E "[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_./:?&=%+@#-]{7,}" case0004/classes*.dex > case0004-strings.txt
wc -l case0004-strings.txt

-a tells grep to read the binary file as text, -o prints only the matched words, and -h hides file names. The pattern keeps every run that starts with a letter and is at least eight characters long.

Expected: wc -l prints a large number. The build used to verify this lab produced about 655,000 lines. The pattern can include unrelated characters at the ends of strings; check these when copying a candidate value.

docs.title: 5. Search for the payment secret
docs.text:
Search the extracted strings for candidate secret names and values:

grep -i "secret" case0004-strings.txt

Expected: a long list. The build used to verify this lab printed 488 hits, mostly identifiers from the bundled Tink and BouncyCastle libraries. Pipe the command into less to page through it, or add | head -n 40 for an initial sample. The payment-secret name and value are near the bottom of the full list.

Look for an uppercase name referring to a payment secret and a long value that resembles a generated key.

Record the name and value in your notes. You may include other suspected leaks in your description, but the required finding is the payment secret.

docs.title: 6. Prove the value ships inside the code
docs.text:
Search for the exact value from step 5 to identify the dex file containing it:

grep -a -l "<the value you copied>" case0004/classes*.dex

Expected: one or more file names, for example case0004/classes.dex. That file travels to every device the app is installed on. If grep prints nothing, the value got cut when you copied it. Copy it again, exactly.

docs.title: 7. Optional: let the project's checker confirm it
docs.text:
If you have the project repository on this machine, run the module's verification script from the repository root with your emulator connected:

bash features/maswe0004/poc/adb_verify.sh

It pulls the installed app again, scans it for known secret formats, and prints what it finds. You can also point it at the file you already have. Pass the path to your copy, because a bare file name only resolves from the folder that holds it:

bash features/maswe0004/poc/adb_verify.sh /path/to/case0004.apk

Expected: [!] CRITICAL VULNERABILITY CONFIRMED (MASWE-0004 / CWE-798): followed by the values it found, including the one you extracted by hand. The script may also flag other hardcoded leftovers in the app. Note anything it caught that your manual search missed.

docs.title: C · Questions
docs.text:
Answer these in your notes before moving on:

  1. ✍️ What made you sure the value you picked was a secret, and not another variable name?
  2. ✍️ Which file inside the package carried it, and why does that file end up on every device that installs the app?
  3. ✍️ What can an attacker do with the value once they have it? Name one concrete action.

docs.title: D · Finding
docs.text:
You have the finding when all three are true:

Test What it shows The keyword search in step 5 The name and the value, found by your own command The exact-value grep in step 6 The same value is a literal string inside classes*.dex, the code that ships to every user Section C, question 3 One sentence of impact: what an attacker does with the value

If you ran step 7, its output is a second, independent confirmation of the same value. Attach it as well.

docs.title: E · Evidence
docs.text:
Hand in:

  1. 📷 Screenshot 1: your terminal with the step 5 command and its hit visible. The name and the full value must be readable; scroll or zoom so neither is cut off.
  2. 📷 Screenshot 2: the step 6 output, or the step 7 script output if you ran it. One of them must tie the value to a file inside case0004/.
  3. ✍️ Two or three sentences, in your own words:
  4. what the secret is,
  5. where it lived in the package,
  6. one concrete thing an attacker could do with it.

Submit these through your training channel. No long report is needed.

docs.title: F · Hints
docs.text:
Hint 1: step 1 or 2 fails
  • Copy the path exactly as printed, without the package: prefix and without surrounding quotes.
  • If pm path prints several lines (split APKs), use the line that ends in base.apk.
  • If adb pull says remote object does not exist, run step 1 again. The path changes after an app update.
Hint 2: step 3 or 4 fails
  • unzip: command not found: use the Windows Explorer workaround in step 3.
  • The strings file ends up empty: check that ls case0004 lists at least one classes*.dex file, and that you are in the folder where you ran step 2.
  • The grep flags in step 4 need Git Bash or any Linux or macOS shell. PowerShell is a different tool and will not run the command as written.
Hint 3: step 5 is noisy or confusing
  • Rerun step 4 if wc -l case0004-strings.txt did not print a large number.
  • Lines that start with L are library type names. Skip them.
  • The pair you want is one name in capitals and one long value with underscores and digits. The requirement mentions payment, so one of the names should mention it too.
  • To shrink the list without reading all of it: grep -i "secret" case0004-strings.txt | grep -i payment.

docs.title: G · Explanation
docs.text:
Open only after sections C and E are done

Complete your answers and capture your evidence before opening the explanation.

Why the secret was in the package

This is CWE-798: Use of Hard-coded Credentials.

The payment secret is a const val in the vulnerable repository class (Maswe0004VulnerableRepository). The compiler embedded its characters in classes.dex as plain text, which is why a keyword search on the shipped file recovered it. Neither a decompiler nor root access was needed.

Why it matters:

  • Anyone who installs or downloads the app can extract the unencrypted value with common tools.
  • A leaked payment secret can lead to fraud or account takeover, depending on what it unlocks.
  • Replacing the hardcoded value requires a new build. Existing APKs still contain the old value.
  • The module demonstrates three more hardcoding habits: secrets in strings.xml or assets, secrets in third-party SDK configuration, and staging endpoints left in release builds.

What the secure app does instead:

The :app-secure implementation fetches short-lived tokens from a backend at runtime and keeps them in memory. It does not embed the backend secret in the package.

Go deeper:

  • Reference page: MASWE-0004: Sensitive Data Hardcoded in the App Package
  • The repository's automation for this module lives in features/maswe0004/poc/: a Semgrep rule for CI scanning, a Frida hook for runtime inspection, and the adb script from step 7.

docs.title: Lab 05: What the Logs Remember
docs.text:
Module MASWE-0005: Sensitive Data Leakage via Logging Category MASVS-STORAGE CWE CWE-532: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File Time ~30 minutes Level Beginner Needs Lab rules read · Lab 00: Setup complete · 🎯 MobSec Victim installed · adb working

Self-paced lab

Inspect the system log, network request logging, and a local log file for sensitive values. Use the demo buttons to produce the output and your terminal to collect it. Section E lists what to submit.

docs.title: A · Requirement
docs.text:
The app should keep credentials, cryptographic keys, and sensitive personal data out of logs. Debugging tools and crash-reporting services can collect those logs, including through bug reports, so a logged value may be copied beyond the app.

Run the first three demonstrations and inspect each output. Identify the sensitive values and explain how someone with access to the logs could use them.

Do not read the project source code. Use the installed app and your terminal.

docs.title: B · Validation
docs.text: Run everything in one terminal (Git Bash on Windows). Inspect the outputs before reading the app's result cards.

docs.title: 1. Clear the log buffer
docs.text:
Clear entries from earlier labs before generating the test output:

adb logcat -c

Expected: no output. The device's log buffer is now empty.

docs.title: 2. Make the app dump its state
docs.text:
Open 🎯 MobSec Victim, expand MASVS-STORAGE, and open the MASWE-0005 row.

Incorrect dashboard subtitle

The row subtitle reads MASWE-0005: Logging (SECURE). That is a bug in this training build. The screen title bar is what counts: MASWE-0005 (VULNERABLE).

The module lists five vectors. This lab uses the first three; the last two belong to the SDK and WebView sinks covered in the reference page.

Tap the first button: 1. Trigger System Console Leak. If a toast complains about a missing attacker app, ignore it; it repeats on every tap, and the leak happens regardless.

docs.title: 3. Inspect the recent log entries
docs.text:
adb logcat -d -t 400 | tail -n 80

Expected: emulator messages and a block of app output marked with a banner. Locate that block in the recent entries.

docs.title: 4. Pull the block out cleanly
docs.text:
Once you have seen the banner, print exactly that block:

adb logcat -d -t 400 | grep -A 25 "CRITICAL APP STATE DUMP"

Expected: the full app-state dump, including device data, personal identifiers, a password, and key material. Record at least two sensitive values and explain what access each could give an attacker.

docs.title: 5. Inspect the network request log
docs.text:
Go back to the module and tap the second button: 2. Trigger Network Leak. The demonstration uses a non-working endpoint, so a request failure is expected. Inspect what the network logger wrote before the connection attempt:

adb logcat -d -t 600 | grep -A 8 "graphql/v2"

Expected: the outgoing request line, followed by its headers. One header starts with Authorization: Bearer and carries a signed token; another carries a CSRF token. A network library printed both because the app enabled full-body logging. The block ends with --> END GET; the failed connection (<-- HTTP FAILED) follows a moment later.

If the grep finds nothing

Some logcat versions move these lines around. Try adb logcat -d -t 600 | grep -i okhttp, then look at the lines around the request.

docs.title: 6. Read the local log file
docs.text:
Tap the third button: 3. Trigger Local File Leak. This demonstration writes to a local file instead of logcat:

adb shell run-as com.hasantuncay.mobsec ls -la files
adb exec-out run-as com.hasantuncay.mobsec cat files/app_debug.log

Expected: a file named app_debug.log, and inside it a line beginning [ERROR] that ends with PAN:, a card number, and CVV:, a three-digit code. The file is plaintext and grows with every tap; the app never deletes it.

docs.title: 7. Optional: let the project's checker confirm it
docs.text:
If you have the project repository on this machine, the module ships a script that repeats these three reads:

bash features/maswe0005/poc/adb_verify.sh

Expected: [!] CRITICAL VULNERABILITY CONFIRMED (MASWE-0005 / CWE-532): followed by the credential line it found in logcat, the token line from the network request, and the payment line from app_debug.log.

docs.title: C · Questions
docs.text:
Answer these in your notes before moving on:

  1. ✍️ The dump contained a password, key material, and personal identifiers. Who or what could collect these values from the log? Compare that access with a file inside the app's private storage.
  2. ✍️ The network request never succeeded, yet its Authorization header is on record. What does that tell you about logging interceptors?
  3. ✍️ app_debug.log is append-only and never cleaned up. What does that mean for the secrets in it over the life of the install?

docs.title: D · Finding
docs.text:
You have the finding when all four are true:

Test What it shows The step 4 output A full app-state dump in the system log, with at least two sensitive values readable The step 5 output A bearer token and CSRF token printed by a network logger before the connection attempt The step 6 output Card data written to a plaintext file that is never deleted Section C, questions 1 to 3 Your explanation of why each sink leaves the app's trust boundary

If you ran step 7, its output is a second, independent confirmation of the same three artifacts. Attach it as well.

docs.title: E · Evidence
docs.text:
Hand in:

  1. 📷 Screenshot 1: your terminal showing the step 4 dump. The password line (or another clearly sensitive line) must be readable.
  2. 📷 Screenshot 2: your strongest of the two other finds: the step 5 network headers or the step 6 file line.
  3. ✍️ Two or three sentences, in your own words:
  4. which sensitive values ended up in which sink,
  5. how logging makes those values available outside the app,
  6. one concrete thing someone with access to the dump could do with it.

Submit these through your training channel. No long report is needed.

docs.title: F · Hints
docs.text:
Hint 1: the log looks empty or the tap did nothing
  • Tap the vector again and dump immediately. Busy emulators rotate the buffer quickly.
  • A toast about the "attacker app" is expected and harmless. The leak does not depend on it.
  • Verify the tag in your output first; every line carries one. It starts with VULN_.
Hint 2: the network grep finds nothing
  • The result card says VULN_NETWORK, but the library prints under OkHttp. Run adb logcat -d -t 800 | grep -i -E "okhttp|Bearer|graphql".
  • The endpoint string is api.internal.company.com; search for that instead of the path.
  • Lines may have scrolled out; tap the button again and repeat within a few seconds.
Hint 3: the file read fails
  • run-as needs the debug build from Lab 00. A release build answers package not debuggable.
  • The file is appended per tap, so tap the button once more, then ls -la files to confirm the name.
  • Copying the line by hand? The number runs to 16 digits; do not cut it short.

docs.title: G · Explanation
docs.text:
Open only after sections C and E are done

Complete your answers and capture your evidence before opening the explanation.

What each vector gives away

MASWE-0005 covers CWE-532: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File.

Vector 1 built a multi-line string with a master key, part of an RSA private key, a full name, a national identification number, an email, and a plaintext password, and handed it to Log.e. Once written, the dump is ordinary log text: readable over adb, copied into bug reports, harvested by any log-collecting pipeline on the device.

Vector 2 sets the OkHttp HttpLoggingInterceptor to Level.BODY. It prints the outgoing request line and headers, including Authorization: Bearer ... and the CSRF token, before attempting the connection. The credentials therefore appear in the log even when the request fails.

Vector 3 writes a payment failure line with a full card number and CVV to app_debug.log in the app's private files. The file is plaintext and never rotated or deleted, so the card data piles up for the life of the install.

Why it matters:

  • Logs cross the app's trust boundary by design: crash reporters, remote logging SDKs, bug reports, and support tooling all read them.
  • A multi-line dump like this one gets copied into bug reports and log pipelines, and those copies outlive the debugging session that produced it.
  • The class in this module covers five sinks in total: the system console, the network stack, a local file, a third-party SDK payload (which logs PII, clipboard content, and message drafts), and a WebView console bridge.

What the secure app does instead:

The :app-secure implementation has a remote kill switch for logging and restricts debug messages to debug builds. It sets the network logger to Level.NONE and uses a redacting interceptor. Diagnostics are encrypted, card numbers are masked, and CVVs are omitted. It replaces raw PII with a salted PBKDF2 hash and forwards only whitelisted WebView console messages.

Go deeper:

  • Reference page: MASWE-0005: Sensitive Data Leakage via Logging
  • The vulnerable code lives in features/maswe0005/src/main/java/com/hasantuncay/mobsec/maswe0005/vulnerable/Maswe0005VulnerableRepository.kt.
  • The module's automation is in features/maswe0005/poc/: a Semgrep rule pack for CI, a Frida hook for runtime inspection, and the adb script from step 7.

docs.title: Lab 06: The Backup That Took Everything
docs.text:
Module MASWE-0006: Sensitive Data Not Excluded From Backup Category MASVS-STORAGE CWE CWE-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor Time ~30 minutes Level Beginner Needs Lab rules read · Lab 00: Setup complete · 🎯 MobSec Victim installed · adb working

Self-paced lab

Check whether the installed app allows backups and which sensitive files are in scope. You will also try a local backup; the result depends on your Android image. Section E lists what to submit.

docs.title: A · Requirement
docs.text:
The app should exclude sensitive files from cloud backups and device-to-device transfers. Backup settings include a manifest flag and rules for individual files. These need to protect the data even when a backup runs without the app open.

Check the installed package's backup flag, then run the demonstrations and inspect the files they create in backup locations. Record the sensitive values and the result of the local backup attempt.

Do not read the project source code. Use the installed app and your terminal.

docs.title: B · Validation
docs.text: Run everything in one terminal (Git Bash on Windows). Ignore the app's result cards and work from the commands on this page.

docs.title: 1. Check the installed package's backup flag
docs.text:
Android tracks whether an app is in scope for backup as a flag on the installed package:

adb shell dumpsys package com.hasantuncay.mobsec | grep -i ALLOW_BACKUP

Expected: one or two lines of the form flags=[ HAS_CODE ALLOW_CLEAR_USER_DATA ALLOW_BACKUP ... ] inside the package's dump; newer images print a matching pkgFlags=[ ... ] line as well. The other flags vary by build; the token ALLOW_BACKUP is the part that matters here. No app interaction is needed to see it.

docs.title: 2. Open the module
docs.text:
Open 🎯 MobSec Victim, expand MASVS-STORAGE, and open the MASWE-0006 row.

Incorrect dashboard subtitle

The row subtitle reads MASWE-0006: Secure Implementation. That is a bug in this training build. The screen title bar is what counts: MASWE-0006 (VULNERABLE).

The module lists four vectors. This lab taps three of them, in this order: the ADB backup vector, the migration vector, and the cloud backup vector. The fourth is covered in section G.

docs.title: 3. The file the ADB backup vector leaves
docs.text:
Tap the second button: 2. ADB Local Backup (adb backup). Then find what it wrote:

adb shell run-as com.hasantuncay.mobsec ls -la files
adb exec-out run-as com.hasantuncay.mobsec cat files/maswe0006_local_backup_vault.db

Expected: a new file maswe0006_local_backup_vault.db, and inside it one line reading SQLITE_SIMULATION: PAN=, a 16-digit card number, a pipe character, then CVV: and three digits.

The .db file is not a database

This demonstration writes a single plaintext line to a file with a .db extension. Read it with cat; a SQLite browser cannot open it as a database.

docs.title: 4. The file the migration vector leaves
docs.text:
Tap the third button: 3. Device-to-Device Migration. Then:

adb exec-out run-as com.hasantuncay.mobsec cat files/maswe0006_migration_credentials.json

Expected: a JSON object with two keys. refreshToken holds a base64 value, and masterKey holds a value starting with 0x. Both are credentials that should be excluded from the migration.

docs.title: 5. The file the cloud backup vector leaves
docs.text:
Tap the first button: 1. Auto Backup — No Exclusion Rules. This one writes to preferences, so list that folder first:

adb shell run-as com.hasantuncay.mobsec ls -la shared_prefs
adb shell "run-as com.hasantuncay.mobsec cat shared_prefs/maswe0006_cloud_backup_session.xml"

Expected: a file named maswe0006_cloud_backup_session.xml with two entries, auth_token (the JWT-looking value again) and user_email, a personal email address in plain text. The write is asynchronous, so if the entry is missing, wait a second and read again.

docs.title: 6. Attempt a local backup
docs.text:
Try creating an archive with the platform's backup command:

adb backup -f maswe0006_loot.ab -noapk com.hasantuncay.mobsec

A dialog appears on the emulator asking to back up your data. Confirm it (no password needed):

Two outcomes are normal:

  • An archive appears. Check it with ls -l maswe0006_loot.ab. The first bytes are readable: head -c 24 maswe0006_loot.ab prints ANDROID BACKUP, which is the format's magic string. You now hold the app's data on your laptop.
  • The platform refuses. On many Android 12 and newer images, adb backup answers Backup disabled or returns an empty file. Record that outcome and continue. Steps 1 through 5 still document the backup flag and sensitive files; this refusal limits what you can demonstrate about local extraction on this image.

docs.title: 7. Optional: let the project's checker confirm it
docs.text:
If you have the project repository on this machine, the module ships a script that repeats the flag check and all four file reads:

bash features/maswe0006/poc/adb_verify.sh

Expected: [!] CRITICAL VULNERABILITY CONFIRMED (MASWE-0006 / CWE-200): followed by the backup flag line, the card data line, the session keys line, and a note about the token and email in preferences. The script prints a bullet for each of the four files it finds in backup scope; it also reads the fourth vector's customer-records file, so tapping that vector adds a line to the report.

docs.title: C · Questions
docs.text:
Answer these in your notes before moving on:

  1. ✍️ With the dumpsys backup flag enabled and no exclusion rules, which backup or transfer channels can copy this app's stored data? Note any platform restrictions you observed.
  2. ✍️ Two files are named .db and .sqlite, and a result card promised a database browser would open them. What is really inside, based on your own output?
  3. ✍️ A backup is made by the user and belongs to the user. Explain why the app should still keep card data out of the archive.

docs.title: D · Finding
docs.text:
You have the finding when all four are true:

Test What it shows The step 1 output The platform has the app flagged as backup-eligible, with no special handling visible in the dump The steps 3 to 5 outputs Card data, session keys, and a personal email sit in plaintext inside files/ and shared_prefs/, the standard backup scope The step 6 outcome Whether local extraction produced an archive with ANDROID BACKUP in its header or was refused; distinguish this result from the flag and file checks Section C, questions 1 to 3 Your explanation of the channels and the impact

If you ran step 7, its output is a second, independent confirmation of the same artifacts. Attach it as well.

docs.title: E · Evidence
docs.text:
Hand in:

  1. 📷 Screenshot 1: the step 1 ALLOW_BACKUP line, plus the file listing from step 3.
  2. 📷 Screenshot 2: the card data line from step 3 and at least one more file read (step 4 or 5).
  3. 📷 Screenshot 3 (only if your image produced an archive): ls -l and the ANDROID BACKUP header.
  4. ✍️ Two or three sentences, in your own words:
  5. which switch is on and which rules are missing,
  6. which sensitive files are in the backup scope,
  7. one concrete way an attacker reaches a backup that the user never noticed.

Submit these through your training channel. No long report is needed.

docs.title: F · Hints
docs.text:
Hint 1: the dumpsys grep prints nothing
  • Older images label the field pkgFlags=. Try adb shell dumpsys package com.hasantuncay.mobsec | grep -i flags and read the lines.
  • If there is no output at all, confirm the app is installed: adb shell pm list packages | grep mobsec.
  • Reading the flag needs no root and no app interaction. If it fails, the package name is wrong.
Hint 2: a file is missing or the folder looks different
  • Vector 1 writes preferences asynchronously; wait a second and list again.
  • shared_prefs and files also hold other modules' artifacts. Look for the exact names: maswe0006_cloud_backup_session.xml, maswe0006_local_backup_vault.db, maswe0006_migration_credentials.json, maswe0006_unencrypted_customer_records.sqlite.
  • run-as: package not debuggable means the release build is installed. Reinstall the debug APK from Lab 00.
Hint 3: the adb backup step misbehaves
  • The on-device dialog must be confirmed. If no dialog appears, the image has the backup service disabled; that is the refusal case described in step 6.
  • If you got an archive and want to look inside, this trick often works in Git Bash: ( printf "\x1f\x8b\x08\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00" ; tail -c +25 maswe0006_loot.ab ) | tar -ztvf - | head -n 30 It may print warnings and exits nonzero after the list, because the truncated stream is expected; your app's file names above the error are the result. If nothing lists, the archive header and size remain your evidence.
  • Keep any output file and record its size, even if the backup failed. Include the refusal message in your notes.

docs.title: G · Explanation
docs.text:
Open only after sections C and E are done

Complete your answers and capture your evidence before opening the explanation.

Why the backup scope was wide

This is MASWE-0006, covering CWE-200 (information exposure) with CWE-312 roots.

The manifest declares android:allowBackup="true" and points at the stock AOSP rule files, backup_rules.xml and data_extraction_rules.xml, with every include and exclude entry still commented out. Net effect: everything the app writes into files/, shared_prefs/, and its databases is in scope for cloud Auto Backup and device-to-device transfer, and dumpsys confirmed the flag on your emulator.

The artifacts show what ended up in that scope. maswe0006_local_backup_vault.db holds PAN=...|CVV=... as a plain text line. maswe0006_migration_credentials.json holds a refresh token and a master key. maswe0006_cloud_backup_session.xml holds a bearer token and a personal email in preferences. A fourth vector (4. Sensitive Data Unencrypted in Backup) writes a customer record with a plaintext password to maswe0006_unencrypted_customer_records.sqlite.

Why it matters:

  • Cloud Auto Backup runs without the app's involvement. A compromised cloud account can leak app data with no device access at all.
  • Device-to-device transfer can copy the stored credentials to a new phone unless the app excludes them.
  • Where supported, adb backup can copy app data to an attached laptop. Android 12 and newer restrict this path for normal apps (targetSdk 31 and up); that restriction does not replace the app's backup flag and exclusion rules.
  • Card data in any of these channels is also a PCI-DSS problem; the standard treats storage and backup together.

What the secure app does instead:

The :app-secure manifest sets android:allowBackup="false", and its rule files explicitly exclude sensitive entries. The secure repository also encrypts its stored data with AES-256-GCM.

Go deeper:

  • Reference page: MASWE-0006: Sensitive Data Not Excluded From Backup
  • The vulnerable code lives in features/maswe0006/src/main/java/com/hasantuncay/mobsec/maswe0006/vulnerable/Maswe0006VulnerableRepository.kt.
  • The module's automation is in features/maswe0006/poc/: a Semgrep rule pack for CI, a Frida hook for runtime inspection, and the adb script from step 7.

docs.title: Lab 07: Encryption in Name Only
docs.text:
Module MASWE-0007: Improper Encryption Category MASVS-CRYPTO CWE CWE-327: Use of a Broken or Risky Cryptographic Algorithm Time ~30 minutes Level Beginner Needs Lab rules read · Lab 00: Setup complete · 🎯 MobSec Victim installed · adb working

Self-paced lab

Collect the demonstrations' outputs from the system log and test what they reveal about the original data. Section E lists what to submit.

docs.title: A · Requirement
docs.text:
The app should use encryption that protects data from someone who lacks the key. That requires an appropriate algorithm and mode, protected keys, and correct use of IVs or nonces. An unreadable output alone does not establish those protections.

Run the demonstrations and collect their log output. Reverse the XOR/Base64 operation to recover the password, then compare repeated AES-CBC ciphertexts and the blocks produced by ECB.

Do not read the project source code. Use the installed app and your terminal.

docs.title: B · Validation
docs.text: Run everything in one terminal (Git Bash on Windows). Ignore the app's result cards; your evidence is your own adb output.

docs.title: 1. Clear the log and open the module
docs.text:
adb logcat -c

Open 🎯 MobSec Victim, expand MASVS-CRYPTO, and open the MASWE-0007 row.

Incorrect dashboard subtitle

The row subtitle reads MASWE-0007: Secure Implementation. That is a bug in this training build. The screen marks itself MASWE-0007 (VULNERABLE).

docs.title: 2. Tap, then read what the app writes
docs.text:
Tap these four buttons, in any order:

  • 1. Broken Algorithm (DES / RC4)
  • 2. Reused / Hardcoded IV (AES-CBC)
  • 4. ECB Mode (Penguin Attack)
  • 7. XOR / Base64 Obfuscation

The module lists seven vectors; this lab uses the four above. Buttons 3, 5, and 6 are covered in section G.

Then dump the module's log stream:

adb logcat -d -s MASWE_0007

Expected: one line per tap, each starting Vector N:. The tag is MASWE_0007, with an underscore. The outputs use Base64 and hex:

  • Vector 1 prints a Base64 string for a DES operation.
  • Vector 2 prints a hex string for an AES-CBC operation.
  • Vector 4 prints two hex blocks joined by B1: ... == B2: ....
  • Vector 7 prints a Base64 string for its "XOR encryption".

The next three checks test whether you can recover plaintext or identify repeated input from these outputs.

docs.title: 3. Reverse the XOR/Base64 operation
docs.text:
Vector 7 applies a constant XOR value to each byte and Base64-encodes the result. Reverse those operations using the constant supplied below.

First, pull the Base64 string out of the log line into a shell variable:

B64=$(adb logcat -d -s MASWE_0007 | grep "Vector 7" | tail -n 1 | sed 's/.*Base64 string: //' | tr -d '\r')
printf '%s\n' "$B64"

Expected: one Base64 string without surrounding log text. Keep it in the shell variable for the decoding command.

Now decode it and flip every byte back with the same constant, 0x5A:

printf '%s' "$B64" | base64 -d | od -An -tu1 | tr ' ' '\n' | grep . | while read -r b; do printf "\\x$(printf '%02x' $((b ^ 0x5A)))"; done; echo

Expected: the original password as readable text. Record how you recovered it without a separately protected key. Include the recovered value in your screenshot, but omit it from the written report.

Where does 0x5A come from?

The constant can be extracted from the app binary using the inspection techniques from Lab 04. Alternatively, try all 256 possible byte values and inspect the decoded outputs for readable text.

docs.title: 4. Compare repeated AES-CBC outputs
docs.text:
Tap 2. Reused / Hardcoded IV (AES-CBC) a second time, then compare its two ciphertexts:

adb logcat -d -s MASWE_0007 | grep "Vector 2" | tail -n 2

Expected: two lines with the same hex string. This AES-CBC demonstration reuses an all-zero IV, so encrypting the same input with the same key produces the same ciphertext. AES-CBC needs a fresh, unpredictable IV for each encryption. With the fixed IV used here, a reader can identify matching plaintexts by comparing ciphertexts.

docs.title: 5. Compare the ECB blocks
docs.text:
Vector 4 encrypts a text block that repeats itself and prints both halves:

adb logcat -d -s MASWE_0007 | grep "Vector 4"

Expected: a line of the form Vector 4: ECB Pattern Leak -> B1: <hex> == B2: <hex> in which the two hex strings are equal. ECB mode encrypts every 16-byte block on its own with no linking, so identical plaintext blocks become identical ciphertext blocks. This is the precondition for the famous ECB penguin picture: patterns in the plaintext stay visible in the ciphertext.

docs.title: 6. Optional: let the project's checker confirm it
docs.text:
If you have the project repository on this machine:

bash features/maswe0007/poc/adb_verify.sh

Expected: [!] CRITICAL VULNERABILITY CONFIRMED (MASWE-0007 / CWE-327): followed by the DES line, the zero-IV line, the ECB line, and a recovered plaintext: line that the script decoded itself. If vectors 3, 5, or 6 were also tapped, it adds a line naming what it captured.

docs.title: C · Questions
docs.text:
Answer these in your notes before moving on:

  1. ✍️ In step 3, you recovered the password using the logged string and a fixed XOR constant. Explain why that operation does not adequately protect the password.
  2. ✍️ In step 4, two encryptions of the same text produced the same output. What was wrong with the IV handling, and what could an attacker learn from the repeated output?
  3. ✍️ All four outputs came from the system log. What logging change would have prevented this way of collecting them? Would that change also fix the encryption weaknesses?

docs.title: D · Finding
docs.text:
You have the finding when all four are true:

Test What it shows The step 2 dump Four "encrypted" outputs, available to anyone reading the log The step 3 output The XOR/Base64 operation reversed to readable text with no key The step 4 output Two identical ciphertexts for repeated input: no randomness in the scheme The step 5 output Equal ciphertext blocks for equal plaintext blocks: ECB leaks structure

If you ran step 6, its output is an independent confirmation of the same artifacts. Attach it as well.

docs.title: E · Evidence
docs.text:
Hand in:

  1. 📷 Screenshot 1: the step 2 dump, showing the four Vector ... lines.
  2. 📷 Screenshot 2: the step 3 commands and their output, with the recovered string readable.
  3. 📷 Screenshot 3: the step 4 comparison, the step 5 line, or both.
  4. ✍️ Two or three sentences, in your own words:
  5. which weaknesses you showed (a fixed XOR constant, a reused IV, and repeated ECB blocks),
  6. why "the output looks unreadable" is not the same claim as "the data is protected",
  7. one real-world consequence of encrypting with a scheme like vector 7's.

Submit these through your training channel. No long report is needed.

docs.title: F · Hints
docs.text:
Hint 1: the log dump is empty
  • The tag is MASWE_0007 with an underscore. -s MASWE-0007 matches nothing.
  • Tap a vector, then dump right away. Running adb logcat -c before your taps keeps the output short.
  • If -s gives you nothing at all, drop it and grep: adb logcat -d | grep MASWE.
Hint 2: the decode step misbehaves
  • Check the extraction first: printf '%s\n' "$B64" must print one clean Base64 string with no spaces or log text around it. If it is empty, re-run the first command and confirm Vector 7 appears in your dump.
  • On macOS, base64 -d is base64 -D; this lab assumes Git Bash.
  • If the output is garbage, your od may not support -An (without it, address offsets get mixed into the byte stream). A text-only fallback with Python: printf '%s' "$B64" | python -c "import base64,sys;print(''.join(chr(b^0x5A) for b in base64.b64decode(sys.stdin.read().strip())))"
  • If you want to skip being told the constant, loop over all 256 values and keep only the line that reads like text: for k in $(seq 0 255); do printf '%s' "$B64" | base64 -d | od -An -tu1 | tr ' ' '\n' | grep . | while read -r b; do printf "\\x$(printf '%02x' $((b ^ k)))"; done; echo " <- k=$k"; done | grep "@"
Hint 3: the script step
  • Run it from the repository root; it needs adb on PATH and the module's vectors already tapped (at least 1, 2, 4, and 7).
  • If it reports nothing found, the log buffer rotated: tap the vectors again and rerun.
  • Exit code 0 means confirmed; 1 means nothing found yet.

docs.title: G · Explanation
docs.text:
Open only after sections C and E are done

Complete your answers and capture your evidence before opening the explanation.

What each button really does

This is MASWE-0007, covering CWE-327 (broken algorithm) with CWE-326 (inadequate strength), CWE-329 (predictable IV), and CWE-323 (key reuse) roots.

The seven demonstrations use these operations:

  1. DES with the key insecure, an eight-byte English word. DES has a 56-bit effective key, which is inadequate for protecting sensitive data.
  2. AES-CBC with the key 1234567890123456 and an all-zero IV, so the output is a pure function of the input.
  3. AES-CBC with the key FixedSecretKey12, a constant IV, and no authentication tag. This pattern can allow padding-oracle attacks when an implementation exposes distinguishable padding errors. The demonstration does not run an oracle.
  4. AES-ECB with the key 16ByteKeyForECB! on a doubled 16-byte block, which is why your two blocks matched.
  5. DES again, with an eight-byte key of all 0x42.
  6. One RSA-2048 pair used both to encrypt and to sign. The pair is generated fresh per tap; the demonstration concerns reuse across purposes, without exposing the key.
  7. XOR with 0x5A plus Base64, the one you reversed by hand.

The symmetric keys and XOR constant listed above are literals in the app binary and can be recovered from the APK using the techniques from Lab 04. The ciphertexts are available in the log. Their unreadable appearance does not show whether the algorithm or key handling protects the original data.

Why it matters:

  • Deterministic encryption leaks equality: equal ciphertexts tell an attacker the plaintexts matched, and chosen-plaintext attacks build on that.
  • ECB reveals repeated blocks in structured data, including records, images, and tokens.
  • CBC without authentication can allow a padding oracle if error responses distinguish padding failures.
  • A hardcoded key can be extracted by anyone who obtains the app package.

What the secure app does instead:

The :app-secure implementation uses AES-256-GCM with a fresh random nonce per operation and separate key material for each purpose. It does not log sensitive values.

Go deeper:

  • Reference page: MASWE-0007: Improper Encryption
  • The vulnerable code lives in features/maswe0007/src/main/java/com/hasantuncay/mobsec/maswe0007/vulnerable/Maswe0007VulnerableRepository.kt.
  • The module's automation is in features/maswe0007/poc/: a Semgrep rule pack for CI, a Frida hook for runtime inspection, and the adb script from step 6.

docs.title: Lab 00: Set up your lab machine
docs.text:
Time ~15 minutes Goal An emulator, a working adb, and the vulnerable app installed You need A laptop · one of the emulators below · the app package (downloaded from the release, or built from source)

Read the lab rules first

The rules that apply to every lab (authorized use, evidence, hints) are on the Labs overview. Read them before you set anything up.

This is a one-time setup. Every other lab assumes these steps are done.

docs.title: Step 1: Get an emulator running
docs.text:
Use one of the two options and stay with it for your labs.

Android Studio emulator
  1. Install Android Studio (the current release; this project is built with AGP 9.2 and SDK 37, so an up-to-date Studio is required).
  2. Open Device Manager → Create device and pick any recent phone (Pixel 7 is a safe choice).
  3. For the system image, choose API 34 or newer.
  4. For later labs, an image without the Google Play Store (for example Google APIs or AOSP) is a good default: the log stays quiet, and adb root is available as a fallback if a step asks for it. Any image works, though: the labs read app-private files through the debug build's run-as, which needs no root.
  5. Finish the wizard and start the emulator.
Genymotion
  1. Install Genymotion with a recent Android image (API 34+).
  2. Start the device.
  3. In the Genymotion settings for that device, enabling root is optional: the labs read app-private files through the debug build's run-as, which needs no root.

docs.title: Step 2: Check adb
docs.text:
Android Studio installs adb with the SDK, usually here:

%LOCALAPPDATA%\Android\Sdk\platform-tools

Add that folder to your PATH, or open a terminal inside it. Then:

adb version
adb devices

You should see something like:

List of devices attached
emulator-5554   device

If adb devices shows unauthorized or nothing

  • unauthorized: accept the debugging prompt on the emulator screen.
  • Empty list: make sure the emulator is fully booted, then run adb devices again.
  • adb: command not found: your terminal does not have platform-tools on PATH.

Run all terminal commands in this course from Git Bash on Windows, or from a normal shell on macOS/Linux.

docs.title: Step 3: Install the vulnerable app
docs.text:
There are two ways to get the app. Use the one that applies to you.

Download the APK

Download app-vulnerable-debug.apk from the lab releases page.

From the terminal, in the folder that contains the APK:

adb install -r app-vulnerable-debug.apk

The release page also lists app-secure-debug.apk and app-attacker-debug.apk. No lab uses those; you only need app-vulnerable-debug.apk.

Build it yourself

From the root of the project repository:

# Windows
gradlew.bat :app-vulnerable:assembleDebug

# macOS / Linux
./gradlew :app-vulnerable:assembleDebug

Then install the built package:

adb install -r app-vulnerable/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-vulnerable-debug.apk

The first build downloads dependencies and can take a while. Android Studio will prompt you to install any missing SDK components.

Both routes end with Success on the terminal.

docs.title: Step 4: Prove your setup works
docs.text:
Run this and read the result:

adb shell pm path com.hasantuncay.mobsec

Expected, a line beginning with package::

package:/data/app/~~<random>/com.hasantuncay.mobsec-<random>/base.apk

Then open the app on the emulator. You should see the 🎯 MobSec Victim app: the screen header reads Vulnerability Dashboard, and the MASVS categories (MASVS-STORAGE, MASVS-CRYPTO, and so on) fill the page.

Setup is done when

  • adb devices lists your emulator as device
  • adb shell pm path com.hasantuncay.mobsec prints a package:/data/app/... path
  • The 🎯 MobSec Victim app opens on the emulator

When all three are true, go to Lab 01: The Token That Stayed in Plain Sight.
